claim: Multiple learning processes contribute to successful goal-directed actions in the face of changing physiological states, biomechanical constraints, and environmental contexts.
source: Multiple learning processes contribute to successful goal-directed actions in the face of changing physiological states, biomechanical constraints, and environmental contexts.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific understanding of motor control.

claim: Implicit sensorimotor adaptation is of primary importance for ensuring that movements remain well-calibrated and accurate.
source: Amongst these processes, implicit sensorimotor adaptation is of primary importance, ensuring that movements remain well-calibrated and accurate.
evidence: This statement reflects the authors' theoretical position based on the literature.

claim: A large body of work on reaching movements has emphasized how adaptation centers on an iterative process designed to minimize visual errors.
source: A large body of work on reaching movements has emphasized how adaptation centers on an iterative process designed to minimize visual errors.
evidence: This claim references existing literature on visuomotor adaptation.

claim: The role of proprioception has been largely neglected in adaptation research, thought to play a passive role in which proprioception is affected by the visual error but does not directly contribute to adaptation.
source: The role of proprioception has been largely neglected, thought to play a passive role in which proprioception is affected by the visual error but does not directly contribute to adaptation.
evidence: This characterizes the state of the field based on review of existing literature.

claim: The proprioceptive re-alignment model (PReMo) proposes that implicit adaptation acts to minimize a proprioceptive error, the distance between the perceived hand position and its intended goal.
source: Here, we present an alternative to this visuo-centric framework, outlining a model in which implicit adaptation acts to minimize a proprioceptive error, the distance between the perceived hand position and its intended goal.
evidence: This is the core theoretical claim of the manuscript, representing the authors' proposed model.

claim: PReMo is consistent with many phenomena that have previously been interpreted in terms of learning from visual errors.
source: This proprioceptive re-alignment model (PReMo) is consistent with many phenomena that have previously been interpreted in terms of learning from visual errors, and offers a parsimonious account of numerous unexplained phenomena.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' theoretical analysis and reinterpretation of existing data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Motor adaptation is an essential feature of human competence, allowing flexible movement in novel and dynamic environments.
source: Motor adaptation is an essential feature of human competence, allowing us to flexibly move in novel and dynamic environments (Kim et al., 2021; Krakauer et al., 2019; Morehead and Orban de Xivry, 2021; Shadmehr et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Motor adaptation relies on multiple learning processes, with a broad distinction between processes that are under conscious control and those that operate outside awareness.
source: Motor adaptation is not a unitary operation but relies on multiple learning processes. Paralleling the memory literature, one broad distinction can be made between processes that are under conscious control and those that operate outside awareness.
evidence: This reflects established understanding in the motor learning literature.

claim: Explicit processes for adaptation are volitional and well-suited for rapid modifications in behavior, while implicit processes occur automatically and operate over a slower time scale.
source: Whereas the former is volitional and well-suited for rapid modifications in behavior, the latter occurs automatically and operates over a slower time scale (Hegele and Heuer, 2010; Huberdeau et al., 2019; McDougle et al., 2016; Werner et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Explicit processes focus on goal attainment, while implicit processes are designed to ensure that the selected movement is flawlessly executed.
source: Computationally, explicit and implicit processes for adaptation are constrained to solve different problems, whereas explicit processes focus on goal attainment, implicit processes are designed to ensure that the selected movement is flawlessly executed (Taylor et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2011.

claim: The deployment of aiming strategies to offset an experimentally imposed perturbation requires prefrontal control.
source: Consistent with this distinction, the deployment of aiming strategies to offset an experimentally imposed perturbation requires prefrontal control (Anguera et al., 2010; Benson et al., 2011; Taylor and Ivry, 2014a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing prefrontal involvement in explicit strategies.

claim: Implicit adaptation is dependent on the integrity of the cerebellum.
source: whereas implicit adaptation is dependent on the integrity of the cerebellum (Butcher et al., 2017; Haar and Donchin, 2020; Hadjiosif et al., 2014; Izawa et al., 2012; Schlerf et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2010; Tseng et al., 2007; Tzvi et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies of cerebellar patients and neuroimaging.

claim: Explicit strategy use is dominant when the error size is large, producing corrective adjustments in reaching direction that scale with the size of the rotation.
source: Explicit strategy use, as measured by verbal aim reports, was dominant when the error size was large, producing corrective adjustments in reaching direction that scaled with the size of the rotation (Figure 1B, adapted from Figure 7A in Bond and Taylor, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Bond and Taylor, 2015, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The extent of implicit adaptation, as measured by no-feedback aftereffects, remains constant for perturbations ranging from 15° to 90°.
source: Yet, the extent of implicit adaptation, as measured by no-feedback aftereffects trials in which participants were instructed to 'move directly to the target' without re-aiming, remained constant for perturbations ranging from 15° to 90°.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Bond and Taylor, 2015, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: While explicit re-aiming can flexibly compensate for errors of varying sizes, implicit adaptation saturates, at least for large errors.
source: Thus, while explicit re-aiming can flexibly compensate for errors of varying sizes, implicit adaptation saturates, at least for large errors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Bond and Taylor, 2015 data.

claim: The visual clamped feedback task provides a method to study implicit adaptation without contamination from explicit processes.
source: The visual clamped feedback task provides an especially striking method to study implicit adaptation without contamination from explicit processes (Morehead et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Morehead et al., 2017.

claim: With clamped feedback, participants adapt despite being fully aware of the manipulation and instructed to always reach directly to the target.
source: Despite being fully aware of the manipulation, participants adapt, with the heading angle shifting in the opposite direction of the rotation in an automatic and implicit manner.
evidence: This describes the key feature of the clamped feedback paradigm.

claim: In clamped feedback tasks, adaptation eventually reaches an upper bound, averaging between 15° and 25° away from the target.
source: Although the size of the visual error never changes, adaptation eventually reaches an upper bound, averaging between 15° and 25° away from the target.
evidence: This is a summary of empirical findings from clamped feedback studies.

claim: The asymptote of implicit adaptation does not vary across a wide range of clamped rotation sizes.
source: Consistent with the results of Bond and Taylor, 2015, this asymptote does not vary across a wide range of clamped rotation sizes (Kim et al., 2018; Neville and Cressman, 2018; Tsay et al., 2022b; Tsay et al., 2021c).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Implicit adaptation in response to visuomotor perturbations has been framed as an iterative process designed to minimize a visual error.
source: Implicit adaptation in response to visuomotor perturbations has been framed as an iterative process, designed to minimize a visual error (Cheng and Sabes, 2006; Donchin et al., 2003; Herzfeld et al., 2014; Kim et al., 2018; Mazzoni and Krakauer, 2006; Morehead et al., 2017; Thoroughman and Shadmehr, 2000; Wolpert et al., 1998).
evidence: This characterizes the dominant theoretical framework in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: According to the visuo-centric view, the extent of implicit adaptation represents a point of equilibrium between learning from visual error and forgetting.
source: According to this visuo-centric view, the extent of implicit adaptation represents a point of equilibrium, one at which the trial-by-trial change in heading angle in response to the visual error is counterbalanced by the trial-by-trial decay ('forgetting') of this modified visuomotor map back to its baseline, default state (Morehead and Smith, 2017; Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the standard state-space model framework, supported by citation.

claim: Several studies have observed that the rate and extent of adaptation saturates for large visual errors.
source: For example, several studies have observed that the rate and extent of adaptation saturates for large visual errors (Kim et al., 2018; Marko et al., 2012; Morehead et al., 2017; Wei and Körding, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: Another hypothesis is that short-term plasticity is limited within the motor system, with the upper bound reflecting the maximum amount of behavioral change the motor system can accommodate.
source: Another hypothesis is that short-term plasticity is limited within the motor system, with the upper bound reflecting the maximum amount of behavioral change the motor system can accommodate (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes an alternative theoretical account, supported by citation.

claim: Deafferented monkeys and humans who have lost their sense of proprioception adapt in a similar manner as control participants.
source: Despite their sensory loss, deafferent individuals adapt in a similar manner as those observed in control participants (Bernier et al., 2006; Sarlegna et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies of deafferented individuals.

claim: Vision alone is sufficient to drive implicit adaptation in deafferented individuals.
source: indicating that vision alone is sufficient to drive implicit adaptation (Blouin et al., 1993; Fleury et al., 1995; Lefumat et al., 2016; Sarlegna et al., 2010; Taub and Goldberg, 1974; Yousif et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from studies of deafferented individuals, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Surgical deafferentation of an upper limb produces severe disorders of movement in monkeys.
source: The classic work of Mott and Sherrington at the end of the 19th Century demonstrated that surgical deafferentation of an upper limb produced severe disorders of movement in the monkey (Mott and Sherrington, 1895).
evidence: This is a historical observation supported by citation.

claim: Humans who suffer neurological disorders resulting in deafferentation have marked deficits in feedback control.
source: Humans who suffer neurological disorders resulting in deafferentation show a surprising capability to produce well-practiced movements, yet these individuals have marked deficits in feedback control (Rothwell et al., 1982; Sanes et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Healthy participants rely almost exclusively on proprioceptive information for rapid feedback control, even when visual information about the limb is available.
source: Indeed, recent work indicates that healthy participants rely almost exclusively on proprioceptive information for rapid feedback control, even when visual information about the limb is available (Crevecoeur et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Crevecoeur et al., 2016.

claim: Deafferented individuals fail to generate specific patterns of isometric and isotonic muscle contractions in a feedforward manner as they initiate rapid elbow flexion.
source: First, deafferented individuals fail to generate specific patterns of isometric and isotonic muscle contractions in a feedforward manner as they initiate rapid elbow flexion (Forget and Lamarre, 1987; Gordon et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies of deafferented individuals.

claim: Neurologically healthy and congenitally blind individuals can adapt to a force-field perturbation without the aid of vision.
source: Second, neurologically healthy and congenitally blind individuals can adapt to a force-field perturbation without the aid of vision, presumably relying solely on proprioceptive input (DiZio and Lackner, 2000; Franklin et al., 2007; Marko et al., 2012; Striemer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: When opposing visual and proprioceptive errors are provided, aftereffects are in the direction counteracting the proprioceptive error instead of the visual error.
source: Third, when opposing visual and proprioceptive errors are provided, aftereffects measured during the no-feedback block after adaptation are in the direction counteracting the proprioceptive error instead of the visual error. Although it is possible that strategic effects extended into the aftereffect block, this result would suggest that proprioceptive errors can be prioritized over visual errors (Hayashi et al., 2020) (also see: Haswell et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hayashi et al., 2020, with a caveat about possible strategic effects.

claim: Individual differences in proprioception are robustly correlated with the extent of implicit adaptation.
source: Fourth, honing in on tasks that have eliminated strategy use, individual differences in proprioception are robustly correlated with the extent of implicit adaptation (Ruttle et al., 2021; Salomonczyk et al., 2013; Tsay et al., 2021a) (but see: Vandevoorde and Orban de Xivry, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies, with a note of a contradictory finding.

claim: Both proprioceptive uncertainty during baseline and proprioceptive biases induced by a visuo-proprioceptive discrepancy are associated with greater aftereffects.
source: That is, both proprioceptive uncertainty during baseline and proprioceptive biases induced by a visuo-proprioceptive discrepancy are associated with greater aftereffects (Features 1 and 3).
evidence: This is a summary statement referring to evidence presented elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: In some models, proprioception is seen as playing a passive role, a signal that is biased by vision but does not drive implicit adaptation.
source: In some models, proprioception is seen as playing a passive role, a signal that is biased by vision but does not drive implicit adaptation (Mattar et al., 2013; Ohashi et al., 2019a; Ohashi et al., 2019b).
evidence: This characterizes existing models in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Other models consider a contribution of proprioception to implicit adaptation, but the computational principles of how this information is used have not been elucidated.
source: Other models consider a contribution of proprioception to implicit adaptation, but the computational principles of how this information is used have not been elucidated (Rossi et al., 2021; Ruttle et al., 2021; Salomonczyk et al., 2013; Zbib et al., 2016).
evidence: This characterizes the state of existing models, supported by citations.

claim: Exposure to a systematic discrepancy between vision and proprioception results in a reciprocal interaction between the two sensory signals.
source: In the case of a visuomotor rotation, exposure to the systematic discrepancy between vision and proprioception results in a reciprocal interaction between the two sensory signals.
evidence: This describes the phenomenon of sensory recalibration.

claim: There is a pronounced shift in the perceived hand position toward the visual cursor, referred to as a proprioceptive shift.
source: As shown in many studies, there is a pronounced shift in the perceived hand position toward the visual cursor, an effect that is referred to as a proprioceptive shift (Burge et al., 2010; Cressman and Henriques, 2010a; Recanzone, 1998; Synofzik et al., 2008; Synofzik et al., 2006; van der Kooij et al., 2013; van der Kooij et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: There is a shift in the perceived location of the cursor towards the hand (visual shift), although this effect is much smaller and less consistently observed.
source: There is also a shift in the perceived location of the cursor towards the hand (i.e. visual shift) (Block and Bastian, 2011; Rand and Heuer, 2019b), although this effect is much smaller and less consistently observed (Simani et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations, with a note about inconsistency.

claim: For large discrepancies between vision and proprioception, the recalibration process does not result in a unified percept, and the shift within each modality saturates.
source: For large discrepancies between vision and proprioception, this recalibration process does not result in a unified percept. Rather the shift within each modality saturates as the visuo-proprioceptive discrepancy increases.
evidence: This describes a key feature of sensory recalibration.

claim: Visuomotor rotations of either 15° or 30° will result in a 5° shift in proprioception toward the visual cursor and a 1° shift in vision towards the actual hand position.
source: For example, visuomotor rotations of either 15° or 30° will result in a 5° shift in proprioception toward the visual cursor and a 1° shift in vision towards the actual hand position (Block and Bastian, 2011; Rand and Heuer, 2019b; Salomonczyk et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Perception of the moving limb is biased towards the direction of the motor command.
source: For instance, perception of the moving limb is biased towards the direction of the motor command (e.g. a visual target) (Bhanpuri et al., 2013; Blakemore et al., 1998; Gaffin-Cahn et al., 2019; Gandevia and McCloskey, 1978; Kilteni et al., 2020; Lanillos et al., 2020; McCloskey et al., 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The cerebellum receives an efference copy of the descending motor command and generates a prediction of the expected sensory consequences of the movement.
source: One model suggests that the cerebellum receives an efference copy of the descending motor command and generates a prediction of the expected sensory consequences of the movement. This prediction is widely relayed to different regions of the brain, providing a form of predictive control (Grüsser, 1994; Sperry, 1950; von Holst and Mittelstaedt, 1950; Wolpert and Miall, 1996).
evidence: This describes a theoretical model supported by citations.

claim: Sensory recalibration effects are enduring and can be observed even when each sensory modality is assessed alone.
source: Sensory recalibration has several notable features: First, sensory recalibration effects are enduring and can be observed even when each sensory modality is assessed alone.
evidence: This describes a key feature of sensory recalibration.

claim: After exposure to a visual perturbation, a visual shift is observed when participants are asked to judge the position of a briefly flashed visual cursor.
source: For instance, after exposure to a visual perturbation, a visual shift is observed when participants are asked to judge the position of a briefly flashed visual cursor (Simani et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Simani et al., 2007.

claim: A proprioceptive shift is observed when participants locate their unseen hand using a touch screen.
source: Similarly, a proprioceptive shift is observed when participants locate their unseen hand using a touch screen (Ruttle et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ruttle et al., 2021.

claim: Both the visual and proprioceptive shift reach asymptotic values within just a few reaches after the introduction of a visuomotor perturbation.
source: These shifts occur rapidly (Ruttle et al., 2016; Ruttle et al., 2021; Ruttle et al., 2018), with both the visual and proprioceptive shift reaching asymptotic values within just a few reaches after the introduction of a visuomotor perturbation (Ruttle et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies by Ruttle and colleagues.

claim: While the extent of recalibration is a fixed ratio for small visuo-proprioceptive discrepancies, the magnitude of the change within each modality exhibits marked saturation.
source: Third, as noted above, while the extent of recalibration is a fixed ratio for small visuo-proprioceptive discrepancies (Zaidel et al., 2011), the magnitude of the change within each modality exhibits marked saturation (Salomonczyk et al., 2013; Tsay et al., 2021b; Tsay et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: According to PReMo, the fundamental error signal driving adaptation is proprioceptive, the mismatch between the perceived and desired hand position.
source: In contrast to visuo-centric models, we propose that the fundamental error signal driving adaptation is proprioceptive, the mismatch between the perceived and desired hand position (Figure 1D, top).
evidence: This is the core theoretical claim of PReMo.

claim: According to PReMo, the upper bound of implicit adaptation will correspond to the point at which the hand is perceived to be aligned with the target.
source: From this perspective, the upper bound of implicit adaptation will correspond to the point at which the hand is perceived to be aligned with the target.
evidence: This is a prediction of PReMo.

claim: Perceived hand position is determined by a multitude of sensory inputs and sensory expectations.
source: As noted above, perceived hand position is determined by a multitude of sensory inputs and sensory expectations.
evidence: This is a foundational assumption of PReMo based on sensory integration principles.

claim: Visual and proprioceptive shifts towards the other modality are global.
source: B. Visual and proprioceptive shifts are global (Rand and Heuer, 2019a; Rand and Heuer, 2020; Simani et al., 2007). This implies that the perceived hand position is not only shifted in the region of space near the biasing source (i.e., the target or feedback cursor), but will also be shifted in the same direction across the workspace (e.g. at the start position).
evidence: This is a principle of PReMo based on empirical observations, supported by citations.

claim: Early in adaptation, the perceived hand position is biased towards the visual cursor due to the proprioceptive shift, resulting in a proprioceptive error.
source: Early in adaptation, the perceived hand position is biased towards the visual cursor due to the proprioceptive shift (Figure 1D, top). This results in a proprioceptive error, the difference between perceived hand position and the visual target, the signal presumed to drive the heading angle of the movement away from the target (and cursor).
evidence: This describes the dynamics of PReMo early in adaptation, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Late in adaptation, the actual position of the hand will reach a point in which the perceived hand is felt at the target, the proprioceptive error is eliminated, and implicit adaptation ceases.
source: Late in adaptation, the actual position of the hand will reach a point in which the perceived hand is felt at the target (Figure 1D, bottom); thus, the proprioceptive error is eliminated, and implicit adaptation ceases.
evidence: This describes the dynamics of PReMo late in adaptation, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: A core observation that spurred the development of PReMo is the intimate link between the proprioceptive shift and extent of implicit adaptation.
source: A core observation that spurred the development of PReMo is the intimate link between the proprioceptive shift and extent of implicit adaptation.
evidence: This describes the empirical motivation for PReMo.

claim: The proprioceptive shift saturates at ~5° and reaches an asymptotic value after only a couple of trials of exposure to a visuo-proprioceptive discrepancy.
source: Across a range of experiments, two notable characteristics stand out: (1) The proprioceptive shift saturates at ~5° and (2) reaches an asymptotic value after only a couple of trials of exposure to a visuo-proprioceptive discrepancy (Block and Bastian, 2011; Cressman and Henriques, 2010a; Gastrock et al., 2020; Modchalingam et al., 2019; Rand and Heuer, 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: Across individuals, the magnitude of the proprioceptive shift is negatively correlated with the extent of adaptation.
source: Across individuals, the magnitude of the proprioceptive shift can be correlated with the extent of adaptation, operationalized as the magnitude of the aftereffect obtained after exposure to a visuomotor rotation (Ruttle et al., 2021; Tsay et al., 2021b) or as the asymptotic change in reaching angle following exposure to visual clamped feedback (Tsay et al., 2021b). As can be seen in Figure 3 (Panels E-G), the magnitude of the shift is negatively correlated with the upper bound of implicit adaptation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The more proprioception shifts towards the cursor position, the greater the extent of implicit adaptation away from the perturbed cursor.
source: That is, the more proprioception shifts towards the cursor position, the greater the extent of implicit adaptation away from the perturbed cursor. A similar pattern has been observed in many other studies (Clayton et al., 2014; Gastrock et al., 2020; Modchalingam et al., 2019; Salomonczyk et al., 2011; Salomonczyk et al., 2013; Simani et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The correlation between proprioceptive shift and the upper bound of adaptation is in accord with PReMo.
source: The correlation between proprioceptive shift and the upper bound of adaptation is in accord with PReMo (Equation 14).
evidence: This is an inference connecting empirical observations to PReMo predictions.

claim: Visuo-centric models of implicit adaptation do not predict the relationship between proprioceptive shift and the upper bound of adaptation.
source: With the focus on the visual error signal, visuo-centric models of implicit adaptation do not consider how the visual perturbation impacts the perceived hand location. Thus, these models do not predict, or rather are moot on the relationship between proprioceptive shift and the upper bound of adaptation.
evidence: This is a critical comparison between PReMo and visuo-centric models.

claim: The rate of implicit adaptation is relatively invariant in response to visual errors that exceed 10°.
source: As can be seen in Figure 4A, the rate (e.g. trial-to-trial change in hand angle) is relatively invariant in response to visual errors that exceed 10°.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PReMo offers a novel account of the saturation effect by shifting the focus from the motor system to the sensory system.
source: PReMo offers a novel account of the saturation effect, one that shifts the focus from the motor system to the sensory system.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the explanatory power of PReMo.

claim: The size of the proprioceptive shift saturates at a common value (~5°) across a wide range of visuo-proprioceptive discrepancies.
source: As noted previously, the size of the proprioceptive shift saturates at a common value (~5°) across a wide range of visuo-proprioceptive discrepancies (Mostafa et al., 2015; Ruttle et al., 2021; Salomonczyk et al., 2013; Synofzik et al., 2008; Synofzik et al., 2010; Synofzik et al., 2006; Tsay et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: The proprioceptive shift is essentially the same following the introduction of a 15° rotation or a 30° rotation.
source: For example, the proprioceptive shift is essentially the same following the introduction of a 15° rotation or a 30° rotation (Tsay et al., 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tsay et al., 2021a.

claim: Since the size of the proprioceptive shift dictates the size of the proprioceptive error, we should expect an invariant rate and extent of motor adaptation in response to visual errors of different sizes.
source: Since the size of the proprioceptive shift dictates the size of the proprioceptive error, we should expect an invariant rate and extent of motor adaptation in response to visual errors of different sizes (Equations 15-17).
evidence: This is a prediction of PReMo based on the saturation of proprioceptive shift.

claim: When the proprioceptive shift scales with the size of small visual errors, the same scaling is mirrored in the extent of implicit adaptation.
source: Even under experimental manipulations for which the proprioceptive shift scales with the size of small visual errors, the same scaling is mirrored in the extent of implicit adaptation ('t Hart et al., 2020), further supporting the link between the proprioceptive shift and implicit adaptation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to 't Hart et al., 2020.

claim: Generalization of implicit adaptation is local, with changes in trajectory limited to targets located near the training region.
source: A core finding is that generalization of implicit adaption is local, with changes in trajectory limited to targets located near the training region (Krakauer et al., 2000; Tanaka et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Many studies have found small, but reliable changes in heading direction to targets that are far from the training location, including at the polar opposite direction of training.
source: More intriguing, many studies have also found small, but reliable changes in heading direction to targets that are far from the training location, including at the polar opposite direction of training (Krakauer et al., 2000; Morehead et al., 2017; Pine et al., 1996; Poh et al., 2021; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: Following an exposure phase with a 45° CCW rotation at one target location, a 5° shift in the CW direction was observed for movements to probe locations more than 135° away.
source: For example, following an exposure phase in which a 45° CCW rotation was imposed on the visual feedback for movements to one target location, a 5° shift in the CW direction was observed for movements to probe locations more than 135° away (Figure 5C, Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2013 and data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Far generalization effects have been hypothesized to reflect some sort of global component of learning, possibly associated with explicit re-aiming.
source: These far generalization effects have been hypothesized to reflect some sort of global component of learning, one that might be associated with explicit re-aiming (Hegele and Heuer, 2010; McDougle et al., 2017; McDougle and Taylor, 2019).
evidence: This describes an existing hypothesis in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Cross-sensory recalibration results in visual and proprioceptive shifts that extend across the training space.
source: Cross-sensory recalibration has been shown to result in visual and proprioceptive shifts that extend across the training space. That is, when proprioceptive judgements are obtained pre- and post-training, the resulting distortions of vision and proprioception are remarkably similar at the trained and probed locations around the workspace (Cressman and Henriques, 2010a; Simani et al., 2007; 't Hart and Henriques, 2016; 't Hart et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: Simani et al., 2007 observed a robust proprioceptive shift at a generalization target 45° from the training location.
source: Specifically, Simani et al., 2007 observed a robust proprioceptive shift at a generalization target 45° from the training location
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Simani et al., 2007.

claim: Studies from the Henriques' group revealed a robust proprioceptive shift as far as 100° from the training target.
source: this finding was extended in studies from the Henriques' group, revealing a robust proprioceptive shift as far as 100° from the training target (Mostafa et al., 2015; 't 't Hart and Henriques, 2016; 't 't Hart et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies from the Henriques group.

claim: PReMo provides a qualitative account of generalization as a combination of a local pattern around the training target and a global pattern attributable to the proprioceptive shift at the start location.
source: PReMo therefore provides a qualitative account of generalization as a combination of (1) a local pattern of generalization of implicit adaptation around the training target caused indirectly by the proprioceptive shift at the target location, and (2) a global pattern of generalization attributable to the proprioceptive shift at the start location.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about how PReMo accounts for generalization patterns.

claim: Perturbed feedback during passive limb movement can drive implicit adaptation.
source: Perturbed feedback during passive limb movement can also drive implicit adaptation. A striking demonstration of this comes from a study by Salomonczyk et al., 2013.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Salomonczyk et al., 2013.

claim: In Salomonczyk et al., 2013, participants showed a proprioceptive shift of around 5° toward the visual cursor following passive movements with perturbed visual feedback.
source: When asked to report their hand position, the participants showed a proprioceptive shift of around 5° toward the visual cursor, comparable to that observed following active movements with perturbed visual feedback in a standard visuomotor rotation paradigm.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to data from Salomonczyk et al., 2013.

claim: After passive perturbation, participants showed a motor aftereffect when instructed to actively reach to the visual target.
source: After the passive perturbation phase, participants were instructed to actively reach to the visual target. These movements showed a motor aftereffect, deviating in the direction opposite to the cursor rotation.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to data from Salomonczyk et al., 2013.

claim: The size of the aftereffect following passive perturbation was correlated with the magnitude of the proprioceptive shift.
source: Moreover, the size of the aftereffect was correlated with the magnitude of the proprioceptive shift (Figure 6B). That is, participants who showed a greater proprioceptive shift toward the visual cursor also showed a stronger motor aftereffect.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Salomonczyk et al., 2013, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PReMo can account for the correlation between a passively induced proprioceptive shift and the magnitude of implicit adaptation.
source: PReMo can also account for the correlation between a passively induced proprioceptive shift and the magnitude of implicit adaptation.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the explanatory power of PReMo.

claim: Visuo-centric models do not provide an account of how the sensorimotor system would be recalibrated in the absence of movement.
source: In contrast, visuo-centric models do not provide an account of how the sensorimotor system would be recalibrated in the absence of movement.
evidence: This is a critical comparison between PReMo and visuo-centric models.

claim: Delaying the visual feedback by as little as 50–100ms can markedly reduce the rate of adaptation.
source: Timing imposes a powerful constraint on implicit adaptation: Delaying the visual feedback by as little as 50–100ms can markedly reduce the rate of adaptation (Held and Durlach, 1992; Held et al., 1966; Kitazawa et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Evidence of implicit adaptation may be negligible if the visual feedback is delayed by more than 2s.
source: Indeed, evidence of implicit adaptation may be negligible if the visual feedback is delayed by more than 2s (Albert et al., 2020; Kitazawa et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Delayed visual feedback also attenuates the proprioceptive shift.
source: Although we have not included temporal constraints in PReMo, it has been shown that delayed visual feedback also attenuates the proprioceptive shift; as such, the model would predict reduced adaptation since the signal driving adaptation is smaller (Equation 4, 6, 8).
evidence: This is an inference connecting empirical observations to PReMo predictions.

claim: The proprioceptive shift is reduced by ~30% for participants for whom the visual feedback on reaching trials was delayed by 750ms.
source: In visuomotor adaptation studies, the proprioceptive shift is reduced by ~30% for participants for whom the visual feedback on reaching trials was delayed by 750ms, relative to those for whom the feedback was not delayed (Debats and Heuer, 2020b; Debats et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies by Debats and Heuer.

claim: In the rubber hand illusion, when visual and tactile feedback are out of phase, participants report less ownership of the rubber hand and exhibit a smaller shift in their perceived hand position toward the rubber hand.
source: Here, timing is manipulated by varying the phase relationship between seeing a brush move along the rubber hand and feeling the brush against one's own arm: When the two sources of feedback are out of phase, participants not only report less ownership of the rubber hand (indexed by subjective reports), but also exhibit a smaller shift in their perceived hand position toward the rubber hand (Rohde et al., 2011; Shimada et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies of the rubber hand illusion.

claim: Implicit adaptation is attenuated when participants are aware of the visual perturbation.
source: Although we have emphasized that adaptation is an implicit process, one that automatically occurs when the perceived hand position is not aligned with the desired hand position, there are reports that this process is attenuated when participants are aware of the visual perturbation.
evidence: This introduces a phenomenon that has been reported in the literature.

claim: Neville and Cressman, 2018 found that participants exhibited less implicit adaptation when they were fully informed about the nature of visuomotor rotation and the strategy required to offset the rotation.
source: For example, Neville and Cressman, 2018 found that participants exhibited less implicit adaptation (indexed by the motor aftereffect) when they were fully informed about the nature of visuomotor rotation and the strategy required to offset the rotation (see also, Benson et al., 2011; but see, Werner et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Neville and Cressman, 2018, with additional citations.

claim: Relative to participants who were uninformed about the perturbation, the extent of implicit adaptation was reduced by ~33% when participants were informed.
source: Relative to participants who were uninformed about the perturbation, the extent of implicit adaptation was reduced by ~33%.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of findings from Neville and Cressman, 2018.

claim: Debats and Heuer, 2020a have shown that awareness of a visuomotor perturbation attenuates the size of the proprioceptive shift.
source: However, Debats and Heuer, 2020a have shown that awareness of a visuomotor perturbation attenuates the size of the proprioceptive shift (Debats and Heuer, 2020a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Debats and Heuer, 2020a.

claim: The magnitude of attenuation of proprioceptive shift by awareness in response to a wide range of perturbations (0° - 17.5°) was around 30%.
source: The magnitude of this attenuation in response to a wide range of perturbations (0° - 17.5°) was around 30%, a value similar to the degree to which implicit adaptation was attenuated by awareness in the Neville and Cressman study.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of findings from Debats and Heuer, 2020a.

claim: A quantitative correspondence in the effect of awareness on proprioceptive shift and implicit adaptation is predicted by PReMo.
source: A quantitative correspondence in the effect of awareness on proprioceptive shift and implicit adaptation is predicted by PReMo (Equation 14).
evidence: This is a prediction of PReMo based on its mathematical formulation.

claim: A core feature of PReMo is that the error signal is the difference between perceived hand position and desired hand position.
source: A core feature of PReMo is that the error signal is the difference between perceived hand position and desired hand position.
evidence: This restates a fundamental principle of PReMo.

claim: Perceived hand position is rarely measured in adaptation studies, perhaps because this variable is not relevant in visuo-centric models.
source: Perceived hand position is rarely measured, perhaps because this variable is not relevant in visuo-centric models.
evidence: This is an observation about the state of the field.

claim: The initial verbal reports of hand position were biased towards the clamped visual feedback by ~5°, but then reversed direction, gradually shifting away from the clamped visual feedback and eventually plateauing at around 1° on the opposite side of the actual target position.
source: The initial responses were biased towards the clamped visual feedback by ~5°, but then reversed direction, gradually shifting away from the clamped visual feedback and eventually plateauing at around 1° on the opposite side of the actual target position (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Tsay et al., 2020b, shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The shape and dynamics of the non-monotonic hand report function are readily accounted for by PReMo.
source: The shape and dynamics of this function are readily accounted for by PReMo.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the explanatory power of PReMo.

claim: The initial shift in hand reports towards the clamp is consistent with the size and rapid time course of the proprioceptive shift.
source: The initial shift towards the clamp is consistent with the size and rapid time course of the proprioceptive shift (Ruttle et al., 2021; Ruttle et al., 2018).
evidence: This connects the observed data to known properties of proprioceptive shift, supported by citations.

claim: The perceived hand position does not asymptote at the actual target location, but rather overshoots the target location by ~1°.
source: Intriguingly, the perceived hand position does not asymptote at the actual target location, but rather overshoots the target location by ~1°.
evidence: This is an observation from the Tsay et al., 2020b data.

claim: The overshoot of the perceived hand position is accounted for by PReMo, as the perceived location of the target is shifted away from the cursor due to visual shift.
source: This overshoot of the perceived hand position is also accounted for by PReMo. During exposure to the rotated visual feedback, not only is the perceived location of the cursor shifted away from the actual cursor position due to cross-sensory recalibration, but this shift is assumed to be a generic shift in visual space, not specific to just the cursor (Simani et al., 2007) (see Feature 1, Corollary 2 above). As such, the perceived location of the target is shifted away from the cursor (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on PReMo, supported by citation.

claim: The overshoot provides a measure of the magnitude of the visual shift, given the assumption that behavior will asymptote when the proprioceptive error is nullified.
source: Indeed, the overshoot provides a measure of the magnitude of this visual shift, given the assumption that behavior will asymptote when the proprioceptive error is nullified (i.e. when the perceived hand position corresponds to the desired hand position: the perceived target location).
evidence: This is an inference based on PReMo's assumptions.

claim: The putative 1° of visual shift inferred from the PReMo parameter fits is consistent with empirical estimates of a visual shift induced by a visuo-proprioceptive discrepancy.
source: Notably, the putative 1° of visual shift inferred from the PReMo parameter fits is consistent with empirical estimates of a visual shift induced by a visuo-proprioceptive discrepancy (Rand and Heuer, 2019b; Simani et al., 2007).
evidence: This connects model predictions to empirical data, supported by citations.

claim: Greater proprioceptive uncertainty/variability is associated with a greater extent of implicit adaptation.
source: As shown in several experiments, greater proprioceptive uncertainty/variability is associated with a greater extent of implicit adaptation (Figure 3H, I, J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Conventional visuo-centric models of implicit adaptation do not account for the relationship between proprioceptive uncertainty and the magnitude of adaptation.
source: As with measures of proprioceptive shift, conventional visuo-centric models of implicit adaptation do not account for the relationship between proprioceptive uncertainty and the magnitude of adaptation.
evidence: This is a critical comparison between PReMo and visuo-centric models.

claim: PReMo predicts that proprioceptive variability will be negatively correlated with implicit adaptation.
source: In contrast, PReMo predicts that proprioceptive variability will be negatively correlated with implicit adaptation (Equation 14).
evidence: This is a prediction of PReMo based on its mathematical formulation. Note: The text says 'negatively correlated' but the data in Figure 3H-J show positive correlations. This may be a terminology issue in the manuscript.

claim: When there is greater uncertainty in the proprioceptive system, the perceived hand position is more biased by the location of sensory expectations from the motor command.
source: When there is greater uncertainty in the proprioceptive system, the perceived hand position is more biased by the location of sensory expectations from the motor command (i.e. the visual target, Equation 4).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on PReMo's principles.

claim: Participants with greater uncertainty in proprioception would require a greater change in their actual hand position to bring their perceived hand position into alignment with the perceived target.
source: Therefore, participants with greater uncertainty in proprioception would require a greater change in their actual hand position to bring their perceived hand position into alignment with the perceived target.
evidence: This is a prediction of PReMo.

claim: In a study by Burge et al., 2008, motor adaptation was attenuated both in rate and asymptotic value when visual feedback was provided as a diffuse Gaussian blob (high uncertainty) compared to a sharply defined cursor (low uncertainty).
source: In a seminal study by Burge et al., 2008, the visual feedback in a 6° (small) visuomotor rotation task was provided in the form of a sharply defined cursor (low uncertainty) or a diffuse Gaussian blob (high uncertainty). In the high uncertainty condition, motor adaptation was attenuated both in rate and asymptotic value.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Burge et al., 2008.

claim: Burge et al., 2008 interpreted the effect of visual uncertainty through the lens of optimal integration, where the learning rate is determined by confidence in sensory prediction and feedback.
source: The authors interpreted this effect through the lens of optimal integration (Burge et al., 2008; Ernst and Banks, 2002), where the learning rate is determined by the participant's confidence in their estimate of the sensory prediction and feedback. When confidence in either is low, the learning rate will be decreased; thus, the added uncertainty introduced by the Gaussian blob reduces the learning rate and, consequently, the asymptotic value of total adaptation.
evidence: This describes the interpretation by Burge et al., 2008, supported by citations.

claim: PReMo predicts an interaction between error size and the effect of visual uncertainty on adaptation.
source: In summary, PReMo, predicts an interaction between error size and the effect of visual uncertainty on adaptation.
evidence: This is a prediction of PReMo.

claim: Visual uncertainty attenuated implicit adaptation when the error size was small (3.5°), but not when the error size was large (30°).
source: Visual uncertainty attenuated implicit adaptation when the error size was small (3.5°), convergent with the results of Burge et al., 2008 (Figure 8B). However, visual uncertainty did not attenuate implicit adaptation when the error size was large (30°) (Tsay et al., 2020a), yielding the predicted interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Tsay et al., 2020a, shown in Figure 8B.

claim: An unpublished study involving participants with low vision and matched controls showed the same interaction, with visual uncertainty due to low vision attenuating implicit adaptation for small errors but not large errors.
source: Nonetheless, more direct evidence that the attenuation stems from uncertainty (and not reward) comes from an unpublished study involving participants with low vision and matched controls, allowing a test of the effect of uncertainty when it comes from an intrinsic source (the individual) rather than manipulating an extrinsic source (the Gaussian cloud) (Tsay et al., 2022d). The results exhibit the same interaction, with visual uncertainty due to low vision attenuating implicit adaptation for small errors but not large errors (despite visual feedback being equated in both groups).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to an unpublished study.

claim: All models of implicit adaptation require a comparison of predicted and observed feedback to derive an error signal.
source: All models of implicit adaptation require a comparison of predicted and observed feedback to derive an error signal.
evidence: This is a general statement about computational models of adaptation.

claim: Extrinsic variability, defined as variability in movement outcomes not attributable to one's own motor output, will reduce one's ability to make accurate sensory predictions.
source: Extrinsic variability, defined here as variability in movement outcomes that are not attributable to one's own motor output, will reduce one's ability to make accurate sensory predictions.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the effects of extrinsic variability.

claim: Albert et al., 2021 found that aftereffects were attenuated by around 30% when participants were exposed to a variable rotation compared to a constant rotation.
source: For example, Albert et al., 2021 compared implicit adaptation (i.e. indexed by motor aftereffects during the washout phase where participants were instructed to forgo any strategy use) in two groups of participants, one exposed to a constant 30° visuomotor rotation and a second exposed to a variable rotation that, across trials, averaged 30° (SD = 12°) (Experiment 7 in Albert et al., 2021). Aftereffects were attenuated by around 30% in the latter condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Albert et al., 2021.

claim: Other studies have found no effect of perturbation variability on adaptation or even an amplified effect on learning from increased perturbation variability.
source: However, these results should be interpreted with caution: Other studies have found no effect of perturbation variability on adaptation (Avraham et al., 2020a; Butcher et al., 2017) or even an amplified effect on learning from increased perturbation variability (Burge et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies with contradictory findings.

claim: The attenuation of adaptation due to uncertainty can emerge from differential sampling of error space relative to a condition with low uncertainty, even when the learning rate is identical.
source: Moreover, the attenuation of adaptation due to uncertainly can emerge from differential sampling of error space relative to a condition with low uncertainty (Tsay et al., 2022c), even when the learning rate is identical for the two conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tsay et al., 2022c.

claim: An impairment in generating a sensory prediction provides one mechanistic account of why individuals with cerebellar pathology show attenuated sensorimotor adaptation.
source: Indeed, an impairment in generating a sensory prediction provides one mechanistic account of why individuals with cerebellar pathology show attenuated sensorimotor adaptation across a range of tasks (Donchin et al., 2012; Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2007; Gibo et al., 2013; Hadjiosif et al., 2014; Izawa et al., 2012; Martin et al., 1996; Parrell et al., 2021; Schlerf et al., 2013; Tseng et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies of cerebellar patients.

claim: PReMo suggests that noisier sensory predictions will result in the actual hand position having a relatively larger contribution to the perceived location of the hand, effectively lowering the upper bound of implicit adaptation.
source: PReMo suggests a specific interpretation: Noisier sensory predictions will result in the actual hand position having a relatively larger contribution to the perceived location of their hand. As such, a smaller change in actual hand position would be required to nullify the proprioceptive error (Equation 14), effectively lowering the upper bound of implicit adaptation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on PReMo.

claim: Evidence from a number of different tasks is consistent with the hypothesis that cerebellar pathology is associated with noisier sensory predictions.
source: Evidence from a number of different tasks is consistent with the hypothesis that cerebellar pathology is associated with noisier sensory predictions (Bhanpuri et al., 2013; Gaffin-Cahn et al., 2019; Therrien and Bastian, 2019; Weeks et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Individuals with cerebellar pathology do not exhibit impairment on measures of proprioception obtained without volitional movement (under static conditions).
source: First, these individuals do not exhibit impairment on measures of proprioception obtained without volitional movement (i.e., under static conditions) (Bhanpuri et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bhanpuri et al., 2013.

claim: The magnitude of the proprioceptive shift in cerebellar patients is comparable to that observed in control participants.
source: Second, the magnitude of the proprioceptive shift in cerebellar patients is comparable to that observed in control participants (Henriques et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Henriques et al., 2014.

claim: Proprioceptive variability appears to be comparable between individuals with cerebellar pathology and matched controls.
source: Third, proprioceptive variability appears to be comparable between individuals with cerebellar pathology and matched controls (Bhanpuri et al., 2013; Weeks et al., 2017a; Weeks et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Several studies have reported sensory shifts following force-field adaptation, with the perceived hand position becoming shifted in the direction of the force-field.
source: In contrast to visuomotor adaptation tasks, there is no manipulation of sensory feedback in a typical force-field study; people see and feel their hand exactly where it is throughout the experiment. Nevertheless, several studies have reported sensory shifts following force-field adaptation (Figure 10A). In particular, the perceived hand position becomes shifted in the direction of the force-field (Mattar et al., 2013; Ohashi et al., 2019a; Ostry et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies and data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: PReMo can account for the shift in perceived hand position in the direction of the force-field.
source: PReMo can account for the shift in perceived hand position in the direction of the force-field.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the explanatory power of PReMo.

claim: Neurologically healthy and congenitally blind individuals can adapt to a force-field perturbation without the aid of vision, with their perceived hand position relying solely on proprioceptive input from the moving limb.
source: Notably, neurologically healthy and congenitally blind individuals can adapt to a force-field perturbation without the aid of vision, with their perceived hand position relying solely on proprioceptive input from the moving limb (DiZio and Lackner, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to DiZio and Lackner, 2000.

claim: Deafferented individuals adapt in response to force-field perturbations, presumably with their perceived hand position dependent on the position of the feedback cursor.
source: Similarly, deafferented individuals also adapt in response to force-field perturbations. Presumably their perceived hand position is dependent on the position of the feedback cursor (Miall et al., 2018; Sarlegna et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies of deafferented individuals.

claim: Force-field adaptation may be fundamentally proprioceptive, with the difference between the perceived and desired hand position constituting the error signal.
source: As such, we suggest that force-field adaptation may be fundamentally proprioceptive. Consistent with the basic premise of PReMo, the difference between the perceived and desired hand position constitutes the error signal to drive force-field adaptation, a process that can operate in the absence of visual feedback.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim extending PReMo to force-field adaptation.

claim: Mattar et al., 2013 found that the degree in which participants adapt to the forcefield is correlated with the amount of proprioceptive shift in the direction of the force-field.
source: Strikingly, Mattar et al., 2013 found that the degree in which participants adapt to the forcefield is correlated with the amount of proprioceptive shift in the direction of the force-field, strengthening the link between the sensory and motor changes that arise during force-field adaptation (also see Feature 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mattar et al., 2013.

claim: PReMo offers a unified account of the motor and perceptual changes observed during force-field and visuomotor adaptation.
source: In summary, PReMo offers a unified account of the motor and perceptual changes observed during force-field and visuomotor adaptation – both of which place emphasis on participants reaching directly to a target.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the scope of PReMo.

claim: Proprioception seems quite relevant for locomotor adaptation where the goal of the motor system is to maintain gait symmetry.
source: Proprioception seems quite relevant for locomotor adaptation where the goal of the motor system is to maintain gait symmetry (Morton and Bastian, 2006; Reisman et al., 2007; Rossi et al., 2019): The misalignment between the desired and perceived gait might serve as a proprioceptive error, triggering implicit locomotive adaptation to restore its symmetry.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of PReMo to locomotor adaptation, supported by citations.

claim: The goal in saccade adaptation is fundamentally visual, to align the eye on a target.
source: In contrast, the goal in saccade adaptation is fundamentally visual, to align the eye on a target (Groh and Sparks, 1996; Grüsser, 1983; Pélisson et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies of saccade adaptation.

claim: The oculomotor system appears to rely on a visual error signal to maintain calibration.
source: The oculomotor system appears to rely on a visual error signal to maintain calibration (Lewis et al., 2001; Noto and Robinson, 2001; Wallman and Fuchs, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies of oculomotor adaptation.

claim: PReMo reframes adaptation in terms of the primary intention of most manual actions, namely, to use our hands to interact and manipulate objects in the world.
source: In the current article, we have proposed a model in which proprioception is the key driver of implicit adaptation. In contrast to the current visuo-centric zeitgeist, we have argued that adaptation can be best understood as minimizing a proprioceptive error, the discrepancy between the perceived limb position and its intended goal. On ecological grounds, our model reframes adaptation in terms of the primary intention of most manual actions, namely, to use our hands to interact and manipulate objects in the world.
evidence: This is a summary of the theoretical motivation for PReMo.

claim: PReMo accounts for a wide range of unexplained, and in some cases, unintuitive phenomena including changes in proprioception during adaptation, phenomenal experience of perceived hand position, the effect of goal and sensory uncertainty on adaptation, and saturation effects.
source: Empirically, the proprioceptive re-alignment model accounts for a wide range of unexplained, and in some cases, unintuitive phenomena: Changes in proprioception observed during both visuomotor and force-field adaptation, phenomenal experience of perceived hand position, the effect of goal and sensory uncertainty on adaptation, and saturation effects observed in the rate and extent of implicit adaptation.
evidence: This is a summary of the empirical support for PReMo.

claim: Much of the key evidence for PReMo comes from correlational studies, particularly the relationship between the magnitude of adaptation and the extent and variability of induced changes in proprioception.
source: It should be emphasized that, to date, much of the key evidence for PReMo comes from correlational studies; in particular, the relationship between the magnitude of adaptation and the extent and variability of induced changes in proprioception following adaptation.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the current evidence base.

claim: Some studies have failed to find significant correlations between measures of proprioception and adaptation.
source: While studies using a wide range of methods have revealed robust correlations between measures of proprioception and adaptation, other studies have failed to find significant correlations (Cressman et al., 2021; Cressman et al., 2010b; Vandevoorde and Orban de Xivry, 2021).
evidence: This acknowledges contradictory findings in the literature, supported by citations.

claim: When proprioception is assessed via subjective reports obtained after an active movement, it may be impossible to dissociate the relative contributions of proprioceptive variability and sensory prediction variability to perceived hand position.
source: For instance, when proprioception is assessed via subjective reports obtained after an active movement, it may be impossible to dissociate the relative contributions of proprioceptive variability and sensory prediction variability to perceived hand position (Izawa et al., 2012; Izawa and Shadmehr, 2011; Synofzik et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a methodological concern, supported by citations.

claim: Rand and Heuer have developed a measure of proprioception based on movement kinematics, without participants being aware of the assessment.
source: Rand and Heuer, for instance, have developed a measure of proprioception that is based on movement kinematics, without participants being aware of the assessment (Rand and Heuer, 2019a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rand and Heuer, 2019a.

claim: The indirect kinematic measure of proprioception shows the signature of a proprioceptive shift with a similar time course as that observed when the shift is measured in a more direct manner.
source: This indirect measure of proprioception shows the signature of a proprioceptive shift with a similar time course as that observed when the shift is measured in a more direct manner.
evidence: This describes a finding from Rand and Heuer's work.

claim: PReMo provides sufficient detail to generate a host of qualitative and quantitative predictions based on a reasonable set of assumptions.
source: Importantly, PReMo provides sufficient detail to generate a host of qualitative and quantitative predictions based on a reasonable set of assumptions.
evidence: This is a claim about the utility and testability of PReMo.

claim: The computation of perceived hand position in PReMo is based on established principles of sensory integration and sensory recalibration.
source: For example, the computation of perceived hand position is based on established principles of sensory integration (Ernst and Banks, 2002) and sensory recalibration (Zaidel et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the theoretical foundations of PReMo, supported by citations.

claim: The key proposition of PReMo, that implicit sensorimotor adaptation operates to reduce a proprioceptive error, is highly ecological.
source: Moreover, the key proposition of PReMo, namely that implicit sensorimotor adaptation operates to reduce a proprioceptive error, is highly ecological.
evidence: This is a claim about the ecological validity of PReMo.

claim: A more direct test of PReMo would involve experimental manipulations of proprioception using brain stimulation methods or tendon vibration.
source: Beyond model comparison and appeals to parsimony, a more direct tack to evaluate the core proposition of PReMo would involve experimental manipulations of proprioception. Brain stimulation methods have been used to perturb central mechanisms for proprioception (Armenta Salas et al., 2018; Balslev et al., 2004; Balslev et al., 2007; Block et al., 2013; Miall et al., 2007) and tendon vibration has been a fruitful way to perturb proprioceptive signals arising from the periphery (Bard et al., 2011; Bernier et al., 2007; Bock and Thomas, 2011; Gilhodes et al., 1986; Goodwin et al., 1972; Layne et al., 2015; Manzone and Tremblay, 2020; Roll et al., 1991).
evidence: This proposes future experimental tests of PReMo, supported by citations to relevant methods.

claim: PReMo would predict that implicit adaptation would be enhanced with greater proprioceptive bias induced by tendon vibration and greater proprioceptive uncertainty via vibrating opposing muscle groups.
source: PReMo would predict that implicit adaptation would be enhanced with greater proprioceptive bias induced by tendon vibration to one muscle group (e.g. vibration to the biceps resulting in illusory elbow extension) and greater proprioceptive uncertainty via vibrating opposing muscle groups (e.g. vibration to biceps and triceps adding noise to peripheral proprioceptive afferents).
evidence: This is a specific prediction of PReMo for future experimental tests.
